position.name: Positions the patient
position.does: sits the patient up with the back exposed
position.normal: The patient is sitting up on the edge of the exam table with the gown open at the back.

general-survey.name: General survey
general-survey.does: looks at the patient: distress, speaking in full sentences, audible wheeze, color
general-survey.normal: Alert and comfortable, in no respiratory distress. Speaks in full sentences. No audible wheeze or stridor. Normal color.

thorax-inspect.name: Inspection of the thorax
thorax-inspect.does: looks at the shape and movement of the chest: symmetry, deformities, retractions, lag, lesions, bruising
thorax-inspect.normal: The chest is symmetric, with no deformities, lesions or bruising. Both sides rise together with no lag, and there are no retractions.

breathing-pattern.name: Respiratory rate, rhythm and effort
breathing-pattern.does: watches the rate, rhythm, depth and effort of breathing and the length of expiration
breathing-pattern.normal: Breathing is quiet, regular and unlabored, with a normal depth and a normal expiratory phase.

accessory-muscles.name: Accessory muscle use
accessory-muscles.does: looks at the neck and abdominal muscles during breathing
accessory-muscles.normal: No use of the sternocleidomastoid or scalene muscles on inspiration, and no abdominal muscle use on expiration.

lips-cyanosis.name: Lips and mouth for cyanosis
lips-cyanosis.does: looks at the lips, tongue and inside of the mouth
lips-cyanosis.normal: Lips, tongue and oral mucosa are pink. No cyanosis.

nails.name: Nail beds for cyanosis and clubbing
nails.does: inspects the fingernails and nail beds
nails.normal: Nail beds are pink with no cyanosis. No clubbing: the normal angle at the nail base is kept, and the nail bed is firm.

ap-diameter.name: Anterior-posterior diameter
ap-diameter.does: compares the front-to-back depth of the chest with its width
ap-diameter.normal: The anterior-posterior diameter is normal, clearly smaller than the side-to-side width. No barrel chest.

chest-wall-palp.name: Palpation of the chest wall
chest-wall-palp.does: palpates the posterior, lateral and anterior chest wall for tenderness, deformity and crepitus
chest-wall-palp.normal: No tenderness, deformity, masses or crepitus over the posterior, lateral or anterior chest wall.

expansion.name: Thoracic expansion
expansion.does: thumbs at the tenth ribs posteriorly, the patient breathes in deeply
expansion.normal: Thoracic expansion is symmetric: both thumbs move apart equally with a deep breath.

fremitus.name: Tactile fremitus
fremitus.does: palpates while the patient says "ninety-nine", posteriorly, laterally and anteriorly, side to side
fremitus.normal: Tactile fremitus is symmetric and normal posteriorly, laterally and anteriorly.

percuss-posterior.name: Percussion, posterior chest
percuss-posterior.does: percusses the back, alternating sides from the top down
percuss-posterior.normal: Posterior chest: resonant and symmetric throughout.

percuss-lateral.name: Percussion, lateral chest
percuss-lateral.does: percusses each side under the arms, alternating sides
percuss-lateral.normal: Lateral chest: resonant and symmetric on both sides.

percuss-anterior.name: Percussion, anterior chest
percuss-anterior.does: percusses the upper lobes and the front of the chest, alternating sides
percuss-anterior.normal: Anterior chest: resonant and symmetric over both upper lobes.

diaphragm-excursion.name: Diaphragmatic excursion
diaphragm-excursion.does: percusses the level of dullness on full expiration and on full inspiration, both sides
diaphragm-excursion.normal: Diaphragmatic excursion is about 4 centimeters on each side, with the diaphragm at the same level on both sides.

ausc-posterior.name: Auscultation, posterior chest
ausc-posterior.does: listens to the back in a ladder pattern, side to side, a full breath at each point
ausc-posterior.normal: Posterior chest: vesicular breath sounds, equal on both sides. No crackles, wheezes, rhonchi or pleural rub.

ausc-lateral.name: Auscultation, lateral chest
ausc-lateral.does: listens under each arm in a ladder pattern, side to side
ausc-lateral.normal: Lateral chest: vesicular breath sounds, equal on both sides. No crackles, wheezes, rhonchi or pleural rub.

ausc-anterior.name: Auscultation, anterior chest
ausc-anterior.does: listens to the upper lobes and the front of the chest in a ladder pattern, side to side
ausc-anterior.normal: Anterior chest: vesicular breath sounds over both upper lobes, bronchovesicular near the sternum. No crackles, wheezes, rhonchi or pleural rub.

egophony.name: Egophony
egophony.normal: No egophony: "ee" sounds like a muffled "ee" over both lungs.

bronchophony.name: Bronchophony
bronchophony.normal: No bronchophony: "ninety-nine" is muffled and indistinct over both lungs.

whispered-pectoriloquy.name: Whispered pectoriloquy
whispered-pectoriloquy.does: listens while the patient whispers "ninety-nine" or "one-two-three"
whispered-pectoriloquy.normal: No whispered pectoriloquy: the whisper is faint and indistinct over both lungs.

trachea.name: Tracheal position
trachea.does: inspects the front of the neck and palpates the trachea

lymph-nodes.name: Cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes
lymph-nodes.does: palpates the neck and above the collarbones for lymph nodes
lymph-nodes.normal: No cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes are palpable.

legs.name: Lower extremities: edema and calves
legs.does: presses over the shins and ankles for pitting, looks at and feels both calves
legs.normal: No pitting edema of the shins or ankles. Both calves are soft, nontender and equal in size.

heart-ausc.name: Heart auscultation
heart-ausc.does: listens over the aortic, pulmonic, tricuspid and mitral areas
heart-ausc.normal: Regular rhythm. Normal first and second heart sounds, with no murmur, rub or extra heart sound.

cases.persona: A 61-year-old shipyard welder, tall and thin, gruff but polite, sitting bolt upright and leaning on his knees, breathing out through pursed lips. He can only get out a few words at a time and gets irritated by long questions. He plays it down ('just my emphysema acting up') but is privately frightened of ending up on oxygen and of losing his job. He is honest about his smoking and a little ashamed of it.
cases.opening: Can't get my breath. This cold went to my chest, and my inhaler isn't touching it.
facts: My grandson gave me a cold last Friday. By Monday it went to my chest. Harder to breathe every day since.
Four days, getting worse. Doesn't let up now, even sitting still.
Like I can't get the air out before I need the next breath. Tight and heavy.
Sitting up, leaning on something. The albuterol used to help. Now it barely does.
Any walking. Talking. Lying down. The coughing fits.
Eight out of ten. Worst it's ever been.
Worse every day since Monday. Mornings are bad till I cough the junk up.
A flare in February. My doctor gave me prednisone and an antibiotic, and I got over it at home. Never been in the hospital for my lungs.
Every morning for years. My smoker's cough. Since Monday it's all day, and I can't stop once I start.
Usually a little white stuff in the morning. Now it's thick, yellow-green, a lot more. Maybe half a cup a day.
Even sitting here. Had to stop twice walking in from the car.
Before this cold, about a block on flat ground, then I'd have to stop for breath. Now I can barely get to the bathroom.
Yes. My wife says I sound like a squeaky toy.
No sharp pain when I breathe. My chest muscles are sore from coughing, that's all.
Felt hot and had chills last night. We don't have a thermometer. No sweats.
Orthopnea and waking up short of breath
Slept in the recliner the last two nights. Easier to breathe and cough sitting up. I don't wake up gasping. Before this I slept flat on one pillow.
No. Ankles skinny as ever. No calf pain.
No trips, no surgery. Sitting around more since Monday, but I get up.
My grandson, he's six, had a bad cold last week. My wife's got the sniffles now too.
Wiped out. Not hungry. No weight loss before this.
Heart's racing since the cold, and the albuterol makes it worse. No chest pressure. No fainting.
Stuffy nose and a sore throat last weekend. Mostly gone.
A little heartburn now and then. Tums take care of it.
No. It's the breathing. My wife made me come. She says I look gray.
Emphysema, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.
Emphysema. They found it six years ago with the breathing test. I did the test again in March, and the lung doctor said my lungs move less than half the air they should.
Hernia repair in 2010. A colonoscopy a few years back.
Just the hernia. Never for my lungs. Never on a breathing machine.
Tiotropium, the Spiriva, every morning for about five years. Albuterol inhaler when I need it. Lisinopril 20 milligrams for my blood pressure, and atorvastatin 40 at night.
Every day. But since Tuesday I've used the albuterol every two hours, more than they told me.
Tums sometimes. A cough syrup this week. No supplements.
Since I was sixteen. A pack a day until two years ago, then half a pack. Had two this morning.
A couple of beers on a Saturday, watching the game.
Welder at the shipyard, thirty-nine years, still working. Lots of fumes and smoke. We didn't wear masks for most of it. I wear one now, mostly.
One-story house. Gas heat. No wood stove. No pets.
With my wife, Carol. Thirty-five years married. She drove me in.
Flu shot last year. Not yet this year. Never had the pneumonia shot.
They tested me at the shipyard years ago. It was fine. Nobody I know has had it.
My mother died of a stroke at 80.
My father had emphysema. He smoked. Died at 72.
My older brother had a heart attack at 66. He's alive. My sister's healthy.
My emphysema acting up from this cold. Same as February, but worse.
That I'll end up on oxygen for good. That I'll lose my job. And I don't want to be a burden on Carol.
Every two hours since Tuesday. It used to last four hours. Now I barely feel it.
Four puffs in the car on the way here.
Just the one in February, treated at home. This is the second.
No. Tired, but my head's clear. Carol says I'm making sense.
Tried the patch once, ten years ago, for a week. I know I should quit. Maybe this is the time.
The lung doctor mentioned a breathing class. I never went.
questions: Am I going to need oxygen at home for good?
Do I have to stay in the hospital?
When can I go back to work?

exam.position: He sits bolt upright on the edge of the stretcher, leaning forward with his hands braced on his knees (tripod position), and cannot lie back.
exam.general-survey: Tall, thin man in moderate respiratory distress. Alert and oriented and answering appropriately, but speaking only in short phrases of four or five words. Breathing out through pursed lips, with an audible expiratory wheeze. A faint bluish tinge to the lips. No sweating.
exam.thorax-inspect: The chest is barrel shaped and symmetric, with no deformities, lesions or bruising. Both sides rise together with no lag. The lower intercostal spaces draw inward with each breath in (paradoxical retraction from the flattened diaphragm).
exam.breathing-pattern: Respiratory rate 28, regular and labored, with pursed-lip breathing and a markedly prolonged expiratory phase.
exam.accessory-muscles: The sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles contract with every breath in, and the abdominal muscles tighten with every breath out.
exam.lips-cyanosis: A faint bluish tinge to the lips and tongue: central cyanosis.
exam.nails: The nail beds are dusky. No clubbing: the normal angle at the nail base is kept, and the nail bed is firm.
exam.ap-diameter: Increased: the front-to-back depth of the chest nearly equals its width (a ratio of about 1.0, above 0.9). Barrel chest.
exam.fremitus: Tactile fremitus is diminished and symmetric posteriorly, laterally and anteriorly.
exam.percuss-posterior: Posterior chest: diffusely hyperresonant and symmetric.
exam.percuss-lateral: Lateral chest: hyperresonant and symmetric on both sides.
exam.percuss-anterior: Anterior chest: hyperresonant and symmetric over both upper lobes.
exam.diaphragm-excursion: Decreased: about 2 centimeters on each side, with the level of dullness low on both sides.
exam.ausc-posterior: Posterior chest: breath sounds diminished and distant throughout both lungs, with diffuse expiratory wheezes, a markedly prolonged expiratory phase, scattered coarse crackles at both bases, and low-pitched rhonchi that partly clear after he coughs. No pleural rub.
exam.ausc-lateral: Lateral chest: distant breath sounds with expiratory wheezes on both sides, and a few coarse crackles low in both axillae.
exam.ausc-anterior: Anterior chest: distant breath sounds over both upper lobes, with expiratory wheezes and a prolonged expiratory phase. No crackles anteriorly.
exam.bronchophony: Transmitted voice sounds are decreased: "ninety-nine" is faint and muffled over both lungs. No bronchophony.
exam.heart-ausc: Distant heart sounds, heard best below the xiphoid in the epigastrium. Regular tachycardia at about 108. No murmur, rub or extra heart sound.

special: neck-veins
Neck vein inspection
looks at the jugular veins with the head of the bed raised, through several breaths
The jugular veins distend with each forced breath out and collapse with each breath in.
mental-status
Mental status and asterixis

Alert and oriented to person, place and time, answering appropriately. No asterixis: the outstretched hands hold steady without flapping.

tests.name: Arterial blood gas
tests.result: Drawn on room air: pH 7.32 (low), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 58 mmHg, partial pressure of oxygen 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 29 mEq/L (high), oxygen saturation 86%. After the first nebulized albuterol and oxygen, he still breathes about 28 times a minute with accessory muscle use.

tests.name: Chest X-ray
tests.result: Hyperinflated, hyperlucent lungs with flattened diaphragms on both sides and a narrow, vertical heart. No infiltrate, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, effusion or mass.
tests.cap: An example of his pattern, not his own film: overinflated, dark lungs with fewer markings, a saber-sheath trachea and a flattened, tented diaphragm (yellow boxes; the labels are the film's own). His film also shows no infiltrate and no pneumothorax.

tests.name: Electrocardiogram (12-lead)
tests.result: Sinus tachycardia at 108. No arrhythmia and no ischemic changes.

tests.name: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP)
tests.result: Normal: 62 picograms per milliliter.

tests.name: Troponin
tests.result: Normal: no rise.

tests.name: Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator (most recent, from his chart)
tests.result: From his clinic chart, March of this year (spirometry is not done during a flare). After the bronchodilator: forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) 2.0 L (47% of predicted), forced vital capacity (FVC) 3.9 L, ratio 0.51; improvement after the bronchodilator under 12%.
tests.cap: An example graph, not his own tracing, with the same numbers as his chart: forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) 2.0 L of a forced vital capacity (FVC) of 3.9 L, a ratio of 0.51, below 0.70: obstruction. Yellow box: the volume-time curve and its ratio.

tests.name: Complete blood count with differential
tests.result: White blood cell count normal at 9,800. Hemoglobin normal at 15.4 grams per deciliter, no anemia. Eosinophils 150 per microliter.

tests.name: D-dimer
tests.result: Negative.

key.diagnosis: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (known severe airflow obstruction: ratio 0.51, forced expiratory volume in 1 second 47% of predicted, grade 3), triggered by a viral cold, with more breathlessness and more, purulent sputum; acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH 7.32, carbon dioxide 58, bicarbonate 29) with resting hypoxemia (saturation 86%, arterial oxygen 52 mmHg), in moderate respiratory distress and still about 28 breaths a minute with accessory muscle use after the first treatments: intensive care admission with noninvasive ventilation
must_not_miss: Worsening hypercapnic respiratory failure: drowsiness, confusion, asterixis, hemodynamic instability, or a falling pH or rising carbon dioxide despite noninvasive ventilation means intubation and invasive ventilation

A second cause hiding behind the exacerbation: pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, acute heart failure or a pneumothorax (the chest X-ray, electrocardiogram, natriuretic peptide, troponin and D-dimer look for them)

ddx.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, acute exacerbation
ddx.support: Known severe disease (ratio 0.51, 47% of predicted), about 44 pack-years and still smoking, 39 years of welding fumes; a cold, then four days of worsening breathlessness (now at rest) with more sputum that turned yellow-green, and albuterol no longer helping. Tripod position, pursed lips, accessory muscle use, barrel chest, central cyanosis, hyperresonance, diminished fremitus and distant breath sounds with wheezes and coarse crackles; saturation 86%, a blood gas with acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis, and a hyperinflated chest X-ray.
ddx.against: Little against it: the low-grade temperature and basal crackles raise pneumonia, which the clear chest X-ray answers.

ddx.name: Pneumonia
ddx.support: A cold, then chills, a temperature of 99.8, purulent sputum and coarse crackles at both bases.
ddx.against: No focal dullness, increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds or egophony (fremitus and voice sounds are decreased everywhere), and no infiltrate on the chest X-ray.

ddx.name: Acute decompensated heart failure
ddx.support: Breathlessness, sleeping in a recliner, basal crackles, high blood pressure and a fast heart rate.
ddx.against: He sits up to breathe and cough, not because he wakes gasping; no leg edema; no third heart sound; neck veins fill only on forced expiration; a normal natriuretic peptide and troponin, and no edema on the chest X-ray.

ddx.name: Pulmonary embolism
ddx.support: Tachycardia and hypoxemia; he does not pass the pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria.
ddx.against: A gradual start after a cold, with purulent sputum; no pleuritic pain, coughing up blood, calf swelling, immobility or surgery; Wells score 1.5 (heart rate only), so unlikely, and the D-dimer is negative.

studies.why: Usually done only in a deteriorating or severe exacerbation: measures oxygenation and carbon dioxide retention, and is repeated after oxygen is started to confirm the oxygen rises without the carbon dioxide rising.
studies.expect: pH 7.32, carbon dioxide 58 mmHg, bicarbonate 29, arterial oxygen 52 mmHg: respiratory acidosis, acute on chronic (for this carbon dioxide the bicarbonate would be about 26 if acute and about 30 if chronic; 29 lies between, and compensation never brings the pH back to normal). Respiratory acidosis is an intensive care criterion, and an arterial oxygen under 55 mmHg needs oxygen.

studies.why: Not diagnostic of the disease, but rules out pneumonia, heart failure and pneumothorax as the cause.
studies.expect: Overinflated, hyperlucent lungs with flattened diaphragms and a narrow, vertical heart; no infiltrate, pneumothorax, edema or effusion.

studies.why: Looks for an arrhythmia (a reason to admit) or ischemia behind the breathlessness; long-acting beta agonists can worsen atrial fibrillation.
studies.expect: Sinus tachycardia at 108; no arrhythmia or ischemic change.

studies.why: Part of the evaluation of every exacerbation: heart failure or a heart attack as the cause of, or a partner in, the breathlessness.
studies.expect: Both normal: natriuretic peptide 62 picograms per milliliter, no troponin rise.

studies.why: Checks for anemia and measures the blood eosinophils, which decide whether an inhaled corticosteroid is added (300 or more).
studies.expect: No anemia, white count normal, eosinophils 150: no inhaled corticosteroid for now.

plan: Oxygen by Venturi mask, which delivers a precise concentration, titrated carefully to a saturation of about 88 to 92% (societies differ; some say at least 90%), since his arterial oxygen is under 55 mmHg and his saturation under 88%; repeat the blood gas to confirm the oxygen rises without the carbon dioxide rising.
Short-acting bronchodilator by nebulizer: albuterol, repeated; continue his tiotropium.

A systemic corticosteroid (oral, or injectable while he is on the mask) and an antibiotic, because the breathlessness came with more sputum that turned purulent. Intravenous, because he needs ventilatory support, even though there is no systemic infection (temperature 99.8, normal white count, clear chest X-ray): doxycycline or a macrolide such as azithromycin, both given intravenously.

Admit to the intensive care unit: respiratory acidosis is an intensive care criterion, and he also meets the admission criteria (marked symptoms despite acute management, still about 28 breaths a minute with accessory muscle use, and a need for noninvasive ventilatory support). Start noninvasive ventilation (bilevel positive airway pressure), which reduces intubation rates and mortality in hypercapnic respiratory failure; he is alert with no asterixis and hemodynamically stable. Repeat the blood gas, intubate only if he worsens, and give prophylaxis against venous clots.
Smoking cessation now: counseling with nicotine replacement, bupropion or varenicline.

Before discharge: add a long-acting beta agonist to his tiotropium (group E after a hospitalized exacerbation), check his inhaler technique, refer to pulmonary rehabilitation, give the yearly influenza vaccine (pneumococcal at 65, or sooner if his lung function falls below 40% or heart disease develops), and arrange follow-up.
education: This is a flare-up of your emphysema. The cold inflamed your already damaged airways, so they are narrower and full of mucus; your oxygen is low and carbon dioxide is building up. A breathing machine with a snug mask will help you blow it off and lowers the chance you need a breathing tube, so you'll stay in intensive care while you're on it.
Stopping smoking, and keeping the welding fumes away from your lungs, are the only things that slow the damage. We will help you quit with counseling and a patch, gum or a medicine.
You will go home on a daily inhaler with two long-acting medicines, plus albuterol for rescue, and we will check how you use them. Don't overuse the albuterol: it strains the heart.

Recovery can take 4 to 6 weeks, and you may not get all the way back to where you were. The breathing class (pulmonary rehabilitation) helps you breathe and move better and keeps you out of the hospital.
Get a flu shot every year. Call 911 for breathlessness at rest that your inhaler doesn't help, blue lips, confusion or sleepiness, or chest pain.
red_flags: Drowsiness, confusion or asterixis (carbon dioxide climbing)
A falling pH or rising carbon dioxide on the repeat gas despite noninvasive ventilation
Hemodynamic instability or a new arrhythmia
After discharge: breathlessness at rest despite the rescue inhaler, blue lips, chest pain or new leg swelling

plan: Clinical diagnosis of uncomplicated acute bronchitis: normal vital signs and oxygen and no focal findings, so no routine chest X-ray, blood count or sputum culture.

No antibiotic, including the azithromycin she asks for, regardless of sputum color or cough duration: call it a chest cold, set the expected course of two to three weeks, and explain that antibiotics do not shorten it and bring side effects, Clostridioides difficile infection and resistance.

Supportive care: rest, fluids and avoiding smoke; acetaminophen for discomfort, with a check of her combination cold products so it is not doubled; no codeine cough syrup and no corticosteroids; pelargonium may ease the cough.
A short trial of a bronchodilator inhaler if the wheeze bothers her; reconsider asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease if the wheeze or cough persists.
Smoking cessation: advise her to quit and offer support; keep away from her husband's smoke.
Vaccines: one dose of 20- or 21-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (cigarette smoking is a risk condition at 19 to 49), the annual influenza vaccine and the updated COVID-19 vaccine.
education: This is a chest cold: a virus irritating the big airways in your chest. Green or yellow mucus does not mean bacteria.

Rest, drink fluids and stay away from smoke. Your DayQuil and NyQuil already contain acetaminophen, the same medicine as Tylenol, so do not take Tylenol on top of them.
Codeine cough syrup barely helps and can make you drowsy and slow your breathing, so please don't take your husband's. This is a good time to quit smoking, and we can help.

studies.why: Abnormal in about 70% of acute embolism; the S1Q3T3 pattern suggests severe right ventricular strain (highly specific, low sensitivity). It also looks for a heart attack.
studies.expect: Sinus tachycardia at 110 with the S1Q3T3 pattern; no ST elevation.

studies.why: Most patients with embolism have an abnormal but nonspecific film (atelectasis, effusion), and the classic signs (focal oligemia, a wedge-shaped opacity, an enlarged descending pulmonary artery) are infrequent; it rules out pneumothorax and pneumonia.
studies.expect: Mild atelectasis at the right base only; no pneumothorax, consolidation or effusion.

studies.why: Risk stratification: a raised troponin or natriuretic peptide in a patient with a normal blood pressure makes it submassive.
studies.expect: Troponin elevated and rising; natriuretic peptide still normal this early.

studies.why: Poor for diagnosing embolism but highly specific for right ventricular strain: a tool for risk stratification. It looks for the D-shaped septum and a clot in the right heart.
studies.expect: Dilated, poorly moving right ventricle with a D-shaped septum; no clot in the right heart.

plan: Start anticoagulation now, on high clinical suspicion while the scan is arranged, unless she is bleeding; confirm with computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (a ventilation-perfusion scan only for kidney failure or a severe contrast allergy).

Risk-stratify: a normal blood pressure, but right ventricular strain on the scan and echocardiogram and a raised troponin make it submassive (intermediate risk). Admit her to a monitored bed: she is at high risk of sudden deterioration, and outpatient treatment is not appropriate with a symptomatic embolism.

Anticoagulation by one of the standard strategies: heparin first (unfractionated by continuous infusion, or low molecular weight heparin), switched after 5 days to dabigatran or edoxaban, or overlapped with warfarin; or rivaroxaban or apixaban alone, starting with a loading dose. Provoked by minor transient risks (estrogen, prolonged travel): 3 to 6 months, with the decision point at 3 months.

Thrombolysis is not routine: in submassive embolism it is controversial, weighing faster right ventricular recovery against major and intracranial bleeding, so a student who weighs it that way is reasoning correctly. It becomes the treatment if she turns massive (systolic pressure under 90 for more than 15 minutes), with thrombectomy if thrombolysis is contraindicated.
Stop the estrogen-containing pill.
Oxygen for her air hunger and mild hypoxemia (saturation 93%), adjusted to her saturation, and pain control.
education: A blood clot formed in your left leg after the long flight, and a large piece of it broke off and lodged in the main artery to your right lung. The estrogen in your pill and sitting still on the plane both made a clot more likely.

The clot is straining the right side of your heart, so you will stay in the hospital on a heart monitor while the blood thinner starts working. Your blood pressure is holding well, and we will watch it closely.

The blood thinner stops the clot from growing and lets your body dissolve it. Because this clot had clear triggers, you will take it for 3 to 6 months, and we will decide at 3 months. Stop your birth control pill: its estrogen raises your risk of another clot.
If you are still short of breath 3 months from now, tell us: the strain on your heart today makes lasting damage to the lung arteries more likely, and we will check for it.

Tell the nurse at once, and later come straight back, for feeling faint, worse breathlessness, more than streaks of blood when you cough, or serious bleeding such as black stools, vomiting blood or a sudden severe headache.
red_flags: Fainting, lightheadedness or a falling blood pressure (circulatory collapse)
Worsening breathlessness or a falling oxygen level
Coughing up more than streaks of blood, or serious bleeding on the blood thinner
key.follow_up: Admission to a monitored bed now; then the 3-month decision point on anticoagulation (provoked by minor transient risks: 3 to 6 months in all), with screening for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension if she is still breathless at 3 months, since right ventricular strain on her first scan is a risk factor for it.
key.presentation: Ms. Castillo is a 34-year-old woman on an estrogen birth control pill, who flew ten hours from Chile nine days ago, presenting with sudden sharp right-sided chest pain with every breath and breathlessness since this morning. She has coughed up blood-streaked sputum twice and has had five days of left calf pain and ankle swelling. She denies fainting, fever, wheeze, prior clots, cancer and surgery. Heart rate 110, respiratory rate 22, saturation 93% on room air, blood pressure 128/78. She is splinting on the right, with a right lower lateral pleural rub that stops on breath-holding and a swollen, warm, tender left calf. My differential is pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pericarditis. Her Wells score is 8.5, so I would go straight to computed tomographic pulmonary angiography, with an electrocardiogram, chest X-ray, troponin, natriuretic peptide and echocardiogram. Diagnosis: submassive pulmonary embolism in the right main pulmonary artery, with right ventricular strain. Plan: heparin, a monitored bed, and stop the estrogen.

high_yield.item: Ask about leg swelling or calf pain, out loud
high_yield.why: It is the pulmonary embolism question: one-sided leg symptoms. Signs of a deep vein thrombosis are worth 3 Wells points, and she did not mention her calf until asked.

high_yield.item: Ask the clotting risks: travel, immobility, surgery, estrogen, pregnancy, cancer and prior clots
high_yield.why: Virchow's triad: a flight over 8 hours and an estrogen pill are hers. Not finding a risk factor should never stop the workup when the picture fits.

high_yield.item: Ask about coughing up blood and fainting
high_yield.why: Pleuritic pain with coughing up blood means a small, pleural-based infarction; fainting would mean circulatory collapse from a massive embolism.

high_yield.item: Examine both legs
high_yield.why: A swollen, warm, tender left calf is the source of the clot and adds 3 Wells points.

high_yield.item: Listen at the right lower lateral chest, then have her hold her breath
high_yield.why: A localized pleural rub goes with the infarction; it stops when she holds her breath, which separates it from a pericardial rub.

high_yield.item: Calculate the Wells score out loud
high_yield.why: Deep vein thrombosis signs 3, embolism as the leading diagnosis 3, heart rate above 100 1.5, coughing up blood 1: 8.5, above 4, so straight to imaging. The pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria and the D-dimer are for scores of 4 or less.

high_yield.item: Risk-stratify before choosing treatment
high_yield.why: Normal blood pressure with right ventricular strain or a raised troponin or natriuretic peptide is submassive, at high risk of sudden deterioration, where thrombolysis is controversial; a systolic pressure under 90 for more than 15 minutes is massive and needs thrombolysis.

high_yield.item: Stop the estrogen and set the length of anticoagulation
high_yield.why: Provoked by minor transient risks (estrogen, a long flight): 3 to 6 months, decided at 3 months.

cases.persona: A 66-year-old retired long-haul truck driver, quiet and matter-of-fact, who smells of cigarette smoke and keeps clearing his throat. He plays it down ('probably just bronchitis') because he is afraid: his father died of lung cancer. He answers questions directly but does not mention the weight loss unless asked. His wife pushed him to come.
cases.opening: This cough won't quit, and my wife made me come in because I've been seeing some blood.
facts: I've had a smoker's cough for years, but three or four months ago it changed. It's there all day now. Then about a month ago I started seeing blood in what I cough up.
It feels like it comes from deep in my chest, maybe more on the left.
The cough is all day, every day now. The blood shows up a few times a week, usually first thing in the morning.
A hacking cough. Some white phlegm, and lately little streaks of bright red blood in it.

Mornings, and the first cigarette of the day. Cold air.
No pain going anywhere. It's a cough, not a pain.
The cough bothers me maybe a four out of ten. The blood is what scares me. A ten was a kidney stone in 2015.
Worst in the morning. A little worse each month.
Never had blood before. Never a cough like this, just the usual morning one.
Yes, all day for three or four months now. Before that, just mornings, for years.
Mostly white, not much. Never yellow or green, and it doesn't smell bad.
Yes, for about a month. Streaks of bright red in the phlegm, a few times a week, never more than a teaspoon. It comes up with the cough. It's not from my nose, and I'm not throwing up.
A little on stairs. Two flights winds me now. It didn't used to.
On flat ground, as far as I want. Two flights of stairs and I have to catch my breath.
No, no pain when I breathe.
No fevers, no chills, no sweats at night.
Yes, eighteen pounds since the summer without trying. I was 180, now I'm about 162. My belt's on a new notch.
Orthopnea and waking up short of breath
No, I sleep flat on one pillow and don't wake up short of breath.
No. I stopped driving two years ago. No long trips, no surgery.
Tired all the time the last couple of months, and not hungry like I used to be. And the weight. No fevers or sweats.
No chest pain, no racing heart, no fainting.
My throat's raw from coughing. No stuffy nose, no drip down the back of my throat.
No, that's about it. My wife made me come because of the blood.
High blood pressure. That's it, that I know of.
Nobody's ever told me I have lung disease. I've never had a breathing test.
A knee scope in 2008. They broke up a kidney stone in 2015.
Just one night for the kidney stone.
Amlodipine 5 milligrams every morning for my blood pressure, about six years.
Cough drops. A cough syrup a while back that didn't do anything. No aspirin, no blood thinners.
Since I was eighteen, a pack a day, sometimes more on the road. I still smoke about a pack a day.
No vaping. Some marijuana in my twenties, nothing since.
Three or four beers a week.
Long-haul truck driver for thirty-five years. Retired two years ago. Lots of diesel fumes at the truck stops.
A 1970s house with a finished basement, where I spend most evenings. Gas heat. No pets. Nobody's ever tested the house for anything.
With my wife, Linda. Our daughter lives in town.
I don't do flu shots. Never had a pneumonia shot.
Not that I know of. Nobody around me has had it. I've never been tested.
My mother had a stroke at 78 and passed at 80.
My father smoked, and he died of lung cancer at 70.
My brother has emphysema. My sister is healthy.
Linda thinks it's cancer, like my dad. I'm hoping it's bronchitis.
Honestly, that it's cancer. I watched what it did to my father.
A doctor mentioned a yearly scan for smokers once, maybe eight years ago. I never went.
About three years ago, for blood pressure refills. The pharmacy's been refilling it since.
No headaches, no trouble with my vision.
No bone pain, no back pain.
No. I'm thinking straight and walking fine.
No pain in my belly on the right. My skin isn't yellow.
My voice is the same as always, and food goes down fine.
Linda says my fingertips look kind of puffy lately. I hadn't noticed.
questions: Is it cancer?
Can't you just give me an antibiotic and see if it clears up?
Do I really have to quit smoking now?

exam.general-survey: Thin man who looks older than his age, alert and comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences with an occasional cough. His clothes hang loose and his belt is cinched to a new hole. Normal color. He smells of cigarette smoke.
exam.nails: Clubbing of the fingers: bulbous swelling of the soft tissue at the nail base, the normal angle between the nail and the proximal nail fold is lost, and the nail beds feel spongy. Nail beds pink, no cyanosis.
exam.fremitus: Tactile fremitus is decreased over the left upper chest, anteriorly below the outer part of the left clavicle and high in the left axilla, compared with the right. Symmetric and normal posteriorly and elsewhere.
exam.percuss-anterior: Anterior chest: dull over the outer part of the left upper chest below the clavicle; resonant over the right upper lobe and elsewhere.
exam.percuss-lateral: Lateral chest: dull high in the left axilla; resonant lower down and on the right.
exam.ausc-anterior: Anterior chest: decreased breath sounds over the dull area of the left upper chest. Vesicular over the right upper lobe. No crackles, wheezes or pleural rub.
exam.ausc-lateral: Lateral chest: decreased breath sounds high in the left axilla; vesicular lower down and on the right. No crackles.

Liver palpation
palpates the right upper abdomen for the liver edge and tenderness
The liver edge is not palpable below the right costal margin, and the right upper abdomen is not tender.

Fundoscopic examination
looks at both optic discs with the ophthalmoscope
Both optic discs have sharp margins. No papilledema.

tests.name: Chest X-ray
tests.result: A 4.5-centimeter mass in the periphery of the left upper lobe with a central lucency (a cavity). No pleural effusion. The right lung is clear.

tests.name: Computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen with contrast
tests.result: A 4.6-centimeter thick-walled, cavitating mass with irregular, spiculated borders in the periphery of the left upper lobe. No enlarged hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes, no pleural effusion, and the liver and adrenal glands are clear.
tests.cap: An example, not his own scan: a large cell carcinoma, a thick-walled cavitating mass in the periphery of the left lung (yellow box). His is also a thick-walled, cavitating mass with spiculated borders, 4.6 centimeters, in the left upper lobe.

tests.name: Positron emission tomography with computed tomography (PET-CT)
tests.result: High uptake in the left upper lobe mass. No uptake in any lymph node or anywhere else in the body.
tests.cap: An example, not his own scan. The four panels are unlabeled, but a round opacity (top right, boxed) sits where a bright focus shows in the two lower panels (boxed). High uptake suggests cancer; inflammation can take it up too. This one is in the right lung; his mass is in the left upper lobe.

tests.name: Biopsy of the mass
tests.result: Not available in this clinic: a specialist takes the biopsy with a needle through the chest wall, guided by computed tomography.

tests.name: Complete blood count with differential
tests.result: Normal: white blood cell count, differential, hemoglobin and platelets normal. No anemia.

tests.name: Comprehensive metabolic panel with calcium and alkaline phosphatase
tests.result: Calcium normal at 9.4 milligrams per deciliter. Sodium normal at 139 mEq/L. Alkaline phosphatase, liver tests, potassium, glucose and kidney function normal.

tests.name: Pulmonary function tests
tests.result: Not available in this clinic: it is done in a pulmonary function laboratory.

tests.name: Sputum acid-fast bacilli smears, mycobacterial culture and rapid molecular test
tests.result: Three sputum specimens collected 8 to 24 hours apart: acid-fast bacilli smears negative and the rapid molecular test for tuberculosis negative. Mycobacterial cultures pending.

key.diagnosis: Lung cancer until the biopsy proves otherwise: a 4.6-centimeter peripheral, cavitating, spiculated left upper lobe mass with high uptake and no lymph node or distant spread, in a 48 pack-year current smoker with coughing up blood, weight loss and clubbing. Most likely a non-small cell cancer (a large, peripheral, cavitated tumor fits large cell carcinoma); if confirmed, stage IIA and a candidate for surgery
must_not_miss: Massive hemoptysis: more than 600 mL in 24 hours is life threatening and needs the emergency department now
Spread beyond the chest or a paraneoplastic syndrome: ask about headache, vision change, bone pain, right upper abdominal pain and confusion, and check the calcium, sodium and alkaline phosphatase

ddx.name: Lung cancer (most likely non-small cell; peripheral cavitating mass)
ddx.support: Over 50, 48 pack-years and still smoking, a father with lung cancer; a chronic cough that changed three to four months ago, a month of blood-streaked sputum, 18 pounds of unintended weight loss, fatigue and new breathlessness on stairs. Clubbing; dullness, decreased fremitus and decreased breath sounds over the left upper lobe. A spiculated, cavitating upper lobe mass over 6 millimeters with high uptake on positron emission tomography.
ddx.against: Not proven until the biopsy: inflammation can also take up the tracer.

ddx.name: Tuberculosis
ddx.support: A cough over 8 weeks, coughing up blood, weight loss, fatigue, and a cavity in an upper lobe, where reactivated tuberculosis tends to cavitate.
ddx.against: No fevers or night sweats, no exposure, a spiculated, thick-walled mass, and negative smears and rapid molecular test (cultures pending).

ddx.name: Lung abscess
ddx.support: A cavitating lesion with cough and coughing up blood.
ddx.against: No fever, and the sputum is scant, white and not foul smelling; months of weight loss and a spiculated mass point to a tumor.

ddx.name: Pulmonary embolism
ddx.support: Coughing up blood with some breathlessness.
ddx.against: Months of gradual symptoms, no sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain or leg swelling, a heart rate of 84 and a saturation of 95%; it explains neither the mass nor the clubbing.

studies.why: Often the first test to show the mass, but not a good tool for working it up; it also rules out other disease.
studies.expect: A 4.5-centimeter peripheral left upper lobe mass with a cavity; no effusion.

studies.test: Computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen with contrast
studies.why: The standard next step: size, borders and location of the mass, the lymph nodes, and the liver and adrenal glands for spread.
studies.expect: A 4.6-centimeter spiculated, cavitating mass in the periphery of the left upper lobe (over 6 millimeters, upper lobe, spiculated, cavitated: all concerning); no enlarged nodes, no effusion, liver and adrenal glands clear.

studies.test: Positron emission tomography with computed tomography
studies.why: Highly metabolic tissue takes up the tracer, suggesting malignancy, and it shows lymph node involvement for staging; inflammation can take it up too.
studies.expect: High uptake in the mass only: no lymph node or distant spread.

studies.why: The biopsy classes the tumor; this peripheral mass is reached with a needle through the chest wall guided by computed tomography, and molecular testing of the tissue follows.
studies.expect: A non-small cell lung cancer; anaplastic, undifferentiated large cells with a negative mucin stain would make it large cell carcinoma.

studies.test: Comprehensive metabolic panel with calcium and alkaline phosphatase
studies.why: Calcium for the hypercalcemia of squamous cell cancer, sodium for the low sodium of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, and alkaline phosphatase and liver tests for spread to bone or liver.
studies.expect: Normal calcium, sodium, alkaline phosphatase and liver tests.

plan: Urgent referral for a biopsy of the peripheral mass with a needle guided by computed tomography, with molecular testing of the tissue.
Pulmonary function tests to judge whether he can tolerate surgery. His blood count with differential and metabolic panel with calcium and alkaline phosphatase are already done and normal.

Until tuberculosis is excluded (a cavitating upper-lobe lesion with coughing up blood and weight loss): a mask on him, airborne precautions with N95 respirators for staff, and isolation ended only on clinical and laboratory criteria; his sputum smears and rapid molecular test are negative, with cultures pending.

Refer to thoracic surgery and oncology: a non-small cell cancer of more than 4 and no more than 5 centimeters without lymph node spread is stage IIA, and stages I to IIIB are resected (lobectomy, or a wedge or segment) if he can tolerate surgery, with chemotherapy, targeted therapy or immunotherapy as adjuncts guided by the tumor's markers.
Smoking cessation today: counseling with nicotine replacement, bupropion or varenicline.
Emergency department for heavy bleeding (more than 600 mL in 24 hours), breathlessness at rest, chest pain or confusion.
education: The scans show a mass in the outer part of your left lung with a hollow center, and it lights up on the special scan the way cancer often does. With your smoking, the blood and the weight loss, I'm worried it is lung cancer, but we can't call it cancer until a small sample is looked at under the microscope.
A specialist will take that sample with a thin needle through your chest wall, using the scanner to guide it.
The scans show no spread to the lymph nodes or anywhere else. If it is cancer, one this size that hasn't spread can often be removed with surgery.
Stopping smoking now matters, and you don't have to do it alone: we have counseling and medicines that help.
Go to the emergency room right away if you cough up more than a few spoonfuls of blood, get short of breath or chest pain, or become confused.
red_flags: Coughing up a large amount of blood (more than 600 mL in 24 hours)
Breathlessness at rest or chest pain
Confusion, seizures or unsteadiness
New bone pain, headache or vision change
key.follow_up: Promptly, with the biopsy arranged as soon as possible and the pulmonary function tests reviewed; then shared care with thoracic surgery and oncology once the biopsy is back.
key.presentation: Mr. Dunmore is a 66-year-old retired truck driver with hypertension and 48 pack-years, still smoking, presenting with three to four months of a changed, persistent cough and a month of blood-streaked sputum, never more than a teaspoon. He has lost 18 pounds without trying and is newly winded on two flights of stairs. He denies fever, night sweats, chest pain, voice change, headaches, bone pain and tuberculosis exposure, and was never screened. His father died of lung cancer. Vital signs are normal, saturation 95%. He has clubbing, and dullness, decreased fremitus and decreased breath sounds over the left upper lobe, without egophony; no lymph nodes. My differential is lung cancer, tuberculosis, lung abscess and pulmonary embolism. Computed tomography shows a 4.6-centimeter spiculated, cavitating peripheral left upper lobe mass with high uptake on positron emission tomography and no nodal spread; sputum tests for tuberculosis are negative. My working diagnosis is lung cancer, likely non-small cell. Plan: guided needle biopsy, pulmonary function tests, surgical referral and smoking cessation.

high_yield.item: Characterize the blood: how much, how often, and where it comes from
high_yield.why: Streaks, never more than a teaspoon, coughed up, not from the nose or stomach; more than 600 mL in 24 hours is massive and life threatening.

high_yield.item: Ask about weight loss and put a number on it
high_yield.why: 18 pounds in four months without trying is a systemic symptom of cancer; tuberculosis would usually bring fevers and night sweats as well.

high_yield.item: Count the pack-years and ask about lung cancer screening
high_yield.why: 48 pack-years and still smoking: he has qualified for a yearly low-dose computed tomography since 55 (ages 55 to 80, 30 or more pack-years, smoking now or quit within 15 years) and never had one.

high_yield.item: Inspect the nails for clubbing
high_yield.why: Loss of the nail-fold angle with a spongy nail bed points to lung cancer; it is rare in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

high_yield.item: Percuss, palpate fremitus and listen side to side over the upper lobes
high_yield.why: Dullness with decreased fremitus and breath sounds over the left upper lobe and no egophony fit a solid mass at the chest wall; consolidation would raise the fremitus and give egophony, and an effusion would sit at the base.

high_yield.item: Palpate the cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes
high_yield.why: Spread to lymph nodes changes the stage and the treatment; his are not palpable.

high_yield.item: Ask about symptoms of spread and of paraneoplastic syndromes
high_yield.why: Headaches, vision change, bone pain, right upper abdominal pain or confusion would mean metastases or low sodium; he has none.

high_yield.item: Ask about tuberculosis exposure, fevers and night sweats
high_yield.why: A cavitating upper lobe lesion keeps tuberculosis on the differential until the sputum smears, rapid molecular test and cultures are back.

cases.persona: A 27-year-old kindergarten teacher, friendly and talkative by nature but now pausing to breathe between short sentences, sitting forward with her hands on her knees. She knows her asthma and her inhalers well. She is a little embarrassed that she stopped her daily inhaler and admits it when asked directly, and she is worried about missing work.

Half my kindergarten class has had runny noses and coughs for two weeks.
I'm tired from not sleeping well. No fevers, no sweats, no weight change.
My heart's been beating fast, especially after I use the inhaler, and it makes me a little shaky. No chest pain, no fainting.
A stuffy nose and a scratchy throat with the cold. My nose is always a bit stuffy in the spring with my allergies. No ear pain.

exam.position: She sits on the edge of the table leaning forward with her hands on her knees and does not want to lie back.
exam.general-survey: Alert, anxious young woman, mildly short of breath at rest, sitting forward with her shoulders hunched. She speaks in short sentences and pauses for a breath between them. Audible expiratory wheeze. Normal color, no cyanosis, no sweating.
exam.breathing-pattern: Respiratory rate 24 and regular, with a markedly prolonged expiratory phase, about twice as long as inspiration. Breathing effort is mildly increased.
exam.fremitus: Tactile fremitus is diminished and symmetric posteriorly, laterally and anteriorly.
exam.percuss-posterior: Posterior chest: diffusely hyperresonant and symmetric.
exam.percuss-lateral: Lateral chest: hyperresonant and symmetric on both sides.
exam.percuss-anterior: Anterior chest: hyperresonant and symmetric over both upper lobes.
exam.diaphragm-excursion: Decreased: about 2 centimeters on each side, with the diaphragm at the same level on both sides.
exam.ausc-posterior: Posterior chest: diffuse high-pitched expiratory wheezes over both lungs with a prolonged expiratory phase. Air movement is reduced but heard at every level. No crackles, rhonchi or pleural rub.
exam.ausc-lateral: Lateral chest: expiratory wheezes on both sides with a prolonged expiratory phase. No crackles.
exam.ausc-anterior: Anterior chest: expiratory wheezes over both upper lobes with a prolonged expiratory phase. No crackles. No inspiratory sound over the neck (no stridor).
exam.heart-ausc: Regular tachycardia at about 108. Normal first and second heart sounds, with no murmur, rub or extra heart sound.

tests.result: Before treatment: 240 liters per minute, 55% of her personal best of 440. After three albuterol and ipratropium nebulizer treatments in the first hour: 330 liters per minute (75%), still 75% an hour after the last treatment. At that recheck she is breathing comfortably and speaking in full sentences, and her lungs are clear with no wheeze.
tests.cap: A: the hand-held peak flow meter. B: normal readings by age and height, men above, women below. Her own best (440 liters per minute) is the number to compare with: 240 before treatment is 55% of it, 330 after treatment is 75%.

key.diagnosis: Acute exacerbation of asthma, moderate (peak flow 55% of her personal best, in the 40 to 69% band), triggered by a viral cold in a patient whose control slipped after she stopped her daily inhaled corticosteroid; good response to treatment, safe for discharge with an action plan
must_not_miss: A severe or life-threatening exacerbation: peak flow under 40%, accessory muscle use or chest retraction at rest, a quiet chest, drowsiness or confusion means oxygen, continuous treatment and transfer to the emergency department
Pulmonary embolism in a breathless, tachycardic woman taking an estrogen pill: ask about sudden onset, pleuritic pain, coughing up blood and a swollen leg

ddx.name: Asthma, moderate acute exacerbation
ddx.support: Known asthma with a classic trigger (a cold from her class) after stopping her inhaled corticosteroid in August; albuterol every 3 to 4 hours with brief relief, waking at 3 in the morning, wheeze, chest tightness and a mostly dry cough. Respiratory rate 24, a prolonged expiratory phase, diffuse expiratory wheezes, diffuse hyperresonance, diminished fremitus and reduced diaphragmatic excursion; swollen nasal mucosa and elbow eczema mark allergic asthma. Peak flow 55% of her best.
ddx.against: Nothing against asthma. Against a severe grade: no accessory muscle use or chest retraction, symptoms only mild at rest, and a peak flow of 55% (the 40 to 69% band), so moderate.

ddx.name: Vocal fold dysfunction
ddx.support: Episodes of noisy, breathless breathing in a young woman.
ddx.against: The noise is an expiratory wheeze over the chest, not an inspiratory stridor over the neck; the hyperresonance and diminished fremitus are air trapping, and her peak flow rose with albuterol.

ddx.name: Pneumonia
ddx.support: Started with a cold; cough, a temperature of 99.0 and a fast heart rate.
ddx.against: Clear-to-white sputum, no fever or chills, no pleuritic pain; no dullness, increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds or egophony over any area, and no infiltrate on the chest X-ray.

ddx.name: Pulmonary embolism
ddx.support: A heart rate of 108, a saturation of 94% and an estrogen birth control pill: she does not pass the pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria.
ddx.against: A gradual start with a cold, a diffuse wheeze that eased with albuterol, and no pleuritic pain, coughing up blood, leg swelling, travel, immobility or surgery; Wells score 1.5 (only the heart rate), so unlikely, and the D-dimer is negative.

studies.why: Grades the exacerbation against her personal best (70% or more good, 40 to 69% moderate, under 40% severe) and is repeated after the first hour of treatment to decide discharge or admission.
studies.expect: 240 liters per minute, 55% of her best of 440: moderate. After three treatments in the first hour, 330 (75%), holding an hour later: a good response.

studies.why: Usually normal or shows hyperinflation in asthma; it looks for another cause of the breathlessness, such as pneumonia or a pneumothorax.
studies.expect: Hyperinflation; no infiltrate, pneumothorax or effusion.

studies.test: Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator
studies.why: The objective measure of airflow, read from her chart rather than repeated during the attack: reversible obstruction (an improvement of 12% or more in the forced expiratory volume in 1 second after albuterol) strongly supports asthma; repeated yearly to monitor.
studies.expect: On file: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 2.2 L (63% of predicted) with a reduced ratio of 0.61, rising 14% to 2.5 L after albuterol: reversible obstruction.

plan: Albuterol by nebulizer, or by metered-dose inhaler with a valved holding chamber, up to three doses in the first hour, with ipratropium added for a moderate exacerbation.
An oral systemic corticosteroid (prednisone) now: a short course, no taper needed.
Oxygen only to keep the saturation at 90% or more; at 94% on room air she needs none now.

Repeat the assessment after the first hour (symptoms, examination, peak flow, saturation): 70% or more of her best, sustained 60 minutes after the last treatment with no distress, means discharge; 40 to 69% is an individual decision about admission; under 40%, drowsiness or confusion means the emergency department and admission.

Discharge on albuterol as needed and the rest of the prednisone course; restart the daily inhaled corticosteroid (fluticasone) with a spacer, check her inhaler technique, and give a written asthma action plan.
The yearly influenza vaccine (caution with the nasal spray in younger patients) and the pneumococcal vaccine; follow-up with primary care or an asthma specialist in 1 to 4 weeks.
education: Your airways are swollen and squeezed tight, and the cold set it off. Stopping the orange inhaler left the swelling untreated, so the albuterol has to work harder and wears off sooner.

Use the orange inhaler every day, even when you feel well: it calms the swelling, and its full effect builds over weeks to months. Use it with a spacer and rinse your mouth afterward to prevent hoarseness and thrush.
Albuterol is your rescue inhaler. Needing it more often than usual means your asthma is out of control, so call us.

Check your peak flow every morning and follow your action plan: 352 or more (80% of your best) is green; 220 to 351 is yellow, so add albuterol and call; under 220 (under 50%) is red, so take your rescue medicine and get help now.
Call 911 if you have trouble walking or talking because of your breathing, if your lips or fingernails turn blue, or if the albuterol is not helping.
red_flags: Trouble walking or talking because of breathlessness
Blue lips or fingernails
Rescue inhaler not helping, or peak flow under 50% of her best
Drowsiness or confusion
key.follow_up: Primary care or an asthma specialist in 1 to 4 weeks to review control, inhaler technique and the action plan; spirometry repeated yearly.
key.presentation: Ms. Kowalski is a 27-year-old teacher with asthma since childhood, presenting with two days of worsening breathlessness, wheeze and chest tightness after a cold. She stopped her daily fluticasone in August and has needed albuterol every three to four hours since yesterday, waking at 3 a.m. two nights running. She denies fever, chest pain, coughing up blood, leg swelling and travel; she takes an estrogen pill and has never smoked. Heart rate 108, respiratory rate 24, saturation 94% on room air. She speaks in short sentences, leaning forward, without accessory muscle use. She has diffuse hyperresonance, diminished fremitus, decreased excursion and diffuse expiratory wheezes with a prolonged expiratory phase. My differential is an asthma exacerbation, vocal fold dysfunction, pneumonia and pulmonary embolism. Peak flow is 55% of her best, a moderate exacerbation; the chest X-ray shows only hyperinflation. Plan: albuterol with ipratropium, oral prednisone, repeat peak flow, then restart her inhaled steroid with an action plan.

high_yield.item: Ask how often she uses her rescue inhaler and whether she takes a daily controller
high_yield.why: Albuterol every 3 to 4 hours and no inhaled corticosteroid since August: frequent bronchodilator use and not taking the inhaled steroid both raise the risk of death, and stopping it is the commonest reason for poor control.

high_yield.item: Ask about past attacks: hospital stays, intensive care, a breathing tube, steroid courses
high_yield.why: A previous near-fatal attack marks the highest risk; hers is one overnight stay at 16 and one prednisone course in February.

high_yield.item: Measure the peak flow and compare it with her personal best
high_yield.why: 55% of her best grades a moderate exacerbation (40 to 69%); 70% or more after treatment, sustained for an hour, allows discharge.

high_yield.item: Look for accessory muscle use and chest retraction, and say how breathless she is at rest
high_yield.why: No accessory muscle use or chest retraction, symptoms only mild at rest and a peak flow of 55% (the 40 to 69% band) make this moderate; severe is symptoms at rest with accessory muscle use, retraction and a peak flow under 40%.

high_yield.item: Listen front and back, side to side, and say what a quiet chest would mean
high_yield.why: Diffuse expiratory wheezes with a prolonged expiratory phase; wheezing fades as the airways close, so a quiet chest in a breathless patient signals a severe exacerbation.

high_yield.item: Percuss and palpate fremitus
high_yield.why: Diffuse hyperresonance, diminished fremitus and reduced excursion are the air trapping of asthma; focal dullness with increased fremitus would point to pneumonia instead.

high_yield.item: Ask about triggers and allergies, and look in the nose and at the skin
high_yield.why: A cold, dust mites, cold air and cats; swollen nasal mucosa and elbow eczema mark allergic (extrinsic) asthma.

high_yield.item: Ask about leg swelling, travel, surgery and estrogen, and examine both legs
high_yield.why: Keeps pulmonary embolism on the differential: she takes an estrogen pill and is tachycardic, so it is weighed and set aside with the history, soft, equal calves with no swelling, and a negative D-dimer.

door.name: Erik Lindqvist
door.cc: I've been getting more and more winded.

cases.persona: A 67-year-old retired mail carrier, gruff, matter-of-fact and slow to complain, who calls himself 'just out of shape'. He sits upright, pauses for breath in long answers, and his wife, who drove him in after a bad night, is in the waiting room. Anything about his heart makes him go quiet: the heart attack scared him more than he admits.
cases.opening: I've been getting more winded for a few weeks, and last night I woke up gasping and couldn't catch my breath for a long time.
facts: About three weeks ago. I noticed it on my walk with the dog, and it's gotten worse every week since.
It's my breathing mostly, but there's a heaviness low on the right side of my chest. (He rests a hand on his right lower ribs.)
It's there all the time now, a little, and a lot worse when I move around or lie down.
Like I can't get a full breath, like the bottom of my right lung is full of something.
Sitting up and resting. Propping myself up at night.
Walking, the steps, carrying the groceries, and lying flat.
A five out of ten sitting here. Last night it was an eight. A ten was my heart attack.
Worse at night when I lie down, and worse each week than the week before. Last night was the worst yet.
A dry cough, mostly at night, for about two weeks.
When I move and when I lie flat. Sitting up here I'm all right, mostly.
Half a block, then I have to stop. Last summer I walked two miles a day with the dog.
Not sharp. Just that heaviness on the right when I take a big breath.
No, the opposite. I'm up about nine pounds in three weeks, and I'm not eating any more than usual.
Orthopnea and waking up short of breath
I'm up to three pillows; I used to sleep on one. I've woken up gasping three times this week, and last night it took a good half hour sitting on the edge of the bed to settle.
Both ankles swell by evening, and my socks leave deep marks. No calf pain; both legs are the same.
Nobody around me has been sick.
Tired. No fevers, no night sweats. I've gained weight, not lost it.
No chest pressure like the heart attack. No racing or skipping, no fainting.
No sore throat, no stuffy nose.
No, I think that's all of it.
High blood pressure for about twenty years, high cholesterol, and the heart attack eight years ago.
No. Nobody ever told me I had emphysema or asthma.
The stent in my heart eight years ago, and a scope on my right knee.
Three days for the heart attack.
Aspirin 81 milligrams, atorvastatin 40 milligrams at night, metoprolol succinate 25 milligrams and lisinopril 10 milligrams in the morning, all for years now.
Every day. My wife fills my pill box.
Tylenol for my knees now and then, and a fish oil pill.
Codeine upsets my stomach. No other allergies.
A pack a day from eighteen until the heart attack at fifty-nine. I quit cold turkey and haven't had one since.
A couple of beers on a Saturday.
Retired mail carrier, thirty-five years walking a route. No asbestos, dust or chemicals that I know of.
A house we've had for thirty years. No mold, no birds.
With my wife, Karin. She drove me here this morning; she's in the waiting room.
A flu shot last month, and the pneumonia shot when I turned sixty-five.
Not that I know of. They tested my skin when I started at the post office, and it was negative.
My mother died of a stroke at seventy-nine.
My father had two heart attacks and died at seventy-one with a weak heart.
A brother, sixty-four, with diabetes, and a sister, seventy, who's healthy.
Karin thinks it's pneumonia. I figured I was just getting old and out of shape.
That it's my heart again. I don't want to go through that again.
Last night was the worst. I woke up gasping and couldn't settle for half an hour, and Karin said that was enough and drove me in this morning.
Eight years ago, crushing pain in the middle of my chest. They put a stent in the front artery. They said the heart muscle took a hit.
I saw the heart doctor for a few years, then he retired, and I never found a new one. Nobody's done an ultrasound of my heart in about five years.
Never had liver or kidney trouble that I know of. My belly isn't swollen, my eyes aren't yellow, and my urine looks normal, not foamy.
No cancer. My last colonoscopy was fine.
A lot of canned soup and deli meat since I retired. I like my salt.
questions: Is this my heart again?
Is it cancer? I smoked for forty years.
Will that fluid come back?

exam.position: He sits up on the edge of the stretcher with the gown open at the back, and says he could not lie flat.
exam.general-survey: Alert and oriented, sitting upright, a little short of breath after moving onto the stretcher but speaking in full sentences. No audible wheeze. Normal color, no sweating.
exam.breathing-pattern: Slightly fast at 22 breaths per minute, regular and a little shallow, with a normal expiratory phase.
exam.thorax-inspect: Symmetric shape with no deformity, lesions or bruising. The right lower chest moves a little less than the left with deep breaths. No retractions.
exam.expansion: Decreased and delayed on the right: the right thumb moves less than the left.
exam.fremitus: Decreased to absent over the right lower back and right lower lateral chest below the tip of the scapula, and slightly increased in a band just above that level. Normal and symmetric elsewhere and over the whole left side.
exam.percuss-posterior: Posterior chest: dull over the right lower back from the tip of the scapula down; resonant above that level and over the whole left back.
exam.percuss-lateral: Lateral chest: dull over the right lower lateral chest; resonant above it and on the left.
exam.diaphragm-excursion: Left: about 4 centimeters. Right: the level of dullness is high, at about the tip of the scapula, and moves only about 1 centimeter between full expiration and full inspiration.
exam.ausc-posterior: Posterior chest: breath sounds absent over the right lower back below the tip of the scapula, with bronchial breath sounds in a band just above that level; vesicular above. A few coarse crackles at the left base that do not clear with a cough. No wheezes or rub.
exam.ausc-lateral: Lateral chest: breath sounds absent over the right lower lateral chest; vesicular above it and on the left. No wheezes or rub.
exam.egophony: Over the right back just above the fluid level, "ee" sounds like "ay" (egophony). Over the fluid itself the voice is faint or absent. No egophony on the left.
exam.bronchophony: Over the fluid at the right base, "ninety-nine" is faint or absent; just above the fluid level it is louder and clearer (bronchophony). Muffled and indistinct over the left.
exam.whispered-pectoriloquy: Over the fluid at the right base the whisper is not heard; just above the fluid level it is louder and clearer (whispered pectoriloquy). Faint and indistinct over the left.
exam.heart-ausc: Regular rhythm at about 96. Normal first and second heart sounds followed by a soft, low-pitched third heart sound at the apex. No murmur or rub.
exam.legs: 2+ pitting edema over both ankles and up both shins to mid-shin, symmetric, with deep sock marks. Both calves are soft, nontender and equal in size.

tests.name: Chest X-ray (upright, frontal and lateral)
tests.result: Moderate right pleural effusion with a meniscus over the lower third of the right chest; blunting of the left costophrenic angle (a small left effusion). Kerley B lines at both bases; the heart is enlarged. Trachea midline. No consolidation, nodule or mass.
tests.cap: An example, not his own film: both costophrenic angles blunted (arrows, yellow boxes), the sign of fluid in the pleural space on an upright film. His shows a moderate right effusion with a meniscus and a small left one.
