tests.name: Chest ultrasound (pleural)
tests.result: A moderate, free-flowing, anechoic right pleural effusion, about 6 centimeters deep at the base, with no septations or loculations and compressed lung above it; a small free-flowing left effusion. A safe site is marked on the right back for thoracentesis.

tests.name: Thoracentesis with pleural fluid analysis (ultrasound-guided)
tests.result: Right side, 800 milliliters of clear, straw-colored fluid removed; breathing easier afterward. Protein 1.8 g/dL, serum 6.8 (ratio 0.26). Lactate dehydrogenase 72 U/L, serum 190 (ratio 0.38); two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum value is 148. No Light's criterion met: a transudate. White cells 420 per microliter, mostly macrophages and lymphocytes. Gram stain: no organisms. Culture: no growth. Cytology: no malignant cells. Chest X-ray afterward: no pneumothorax.

tests.name: Comprehensive metabolic panel with serum protein and lactate dehydrogenase
tests.result: Drawn with the tap: total protein 6.8 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 190 U/L (upper limit of normal 222). Albumin 3.9 g/dL, normal. Sodium 136, potassium 4.2, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL; liver tests normal.

tests.name: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP)
tests.result: Highly elevated: about 1,100 picograms per milliliter.

tests.name: Echocardiogram (transthoracic)
tests.result: Dilated left ventricle with an akinetic anterior wall and apex; ejection fraction about 30%. Normal right ventricle; no significant valve disease. Moderate right and small left pleural effusions.

tests.name: Electrocardiogram (12-lead)
tests.result: Sinus rhythm at 96. Q waves in V1 to V4 from an old anterior infarction; no acute ST elevation or depression.

tests.name: Complete blood count (CBC)
tests.result: Normal: white blood cell count 7,400 with a normal differential, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, platelets normal.

key.diagnosis: Moderate right pleural effusion with a small left effusion, a transudate by Light's criteria, from newly diagnosed, decompensated heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction (ischemic cardiomyopathy after his old heart attack)
must_not_miss: Infected fluid (a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema): fever, sharp pleuritic pain or cloudy, purulent fluid needs prompt drainage and antibiotics
Malignant pleural effusion in a 41 pack-year former smoker: the cytology is checked, and an effusion that persists despite treatment of the heart failure is looked at again

ddx.name: Pleural effusion (transudate) from heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
ddx.support: Three weeks of worsening exertional breathlessness, now at half a block, three-pillow orthopnea, waking up gasping, a nine-pound weight gain and symmetric ankle edema after a heart attack eight years ago. A third heart sound and left basal crackles. The right base lags, with absent fremitus, dullness, a high, barely moving diaphragm, absent breath sounds and voice sounds that return just above the fluid. Kerley B lines, a transudate by Light's criteria, a natriuretic peptide above 900 and an ejection fraction of 30%.
ddx.against: Nothing on the examination or in the fluid. His effusion is mostly on the right with a small left one, which is why the fluid was tapped rather than assumed.

ddx.name: Malignant pleural effusion
ddx.support: A 41 pack-year smoking history with a new effusion and a cough.
ddx.against: No weight loss, coughing up blood or night sweats; no mass on the X-ray; the fluid is a transudate (cancer gives an exudate) with no malignant cells.

ddx.name: Parapneumonic effusion from pneumonia
ddx.support: A cough with a new effusion.
ddx.against: No fever, chills, purulent sputum or sharp pleuritic pain; a normal white count; a transudate with a negative Gram stain and culture.

ddx.name: Low-albumin transudate (cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome)
ddx.support: A transudate with leg swelling.
ddx.against: Normal albumin, no liver disease, little alcohol, no belly swelling or foamy urine; orthopnea, waking up gasping and a third heart sound point to the heart.

studies.test: Chest X-ray, upright frontal and lateral
studies.why: Confirms the effusion, its side and size (75 milliliters blunts the posterior angle, 175 the lateral), and looks for a cause: Kerley B lines, a mass or pneumonia.
studies.expect: Moderate right effusion, small left effusion, Kerley B lines, an enlarged heart; no consolidation or mass.

studies.why: Has replaced the lateral decubitus film: shows whether the fluid is free-flowing or loculated and guides the thoracentesis.
studies.expect: Free-flowing right effusion about 6 centimeters deep, no loculations; small left effusion.

studies.test: Thoracentesis with fluid analysis, plus serum protein and lactate dehydrogenase the same day
studies.why: Tapped because the effusion is new and lopsided and he has no known heart failure, so there is no established cause yet; it also relieves his breathing. Send protein, lactate dehydrogenase, white count with differential, Gram stain, cytology and culture. Light's criteria: exudate if any one of fluid-to-serum protein above 0.5, fluid-to-serum lactate dehydrogenase above 0.6, or fluid lactate dehydrogenase above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum; transudate if none.
studies.expect: Clear, straw-colored fluid; protein ratio 0.26, lactate dehydrogenase ratio 0.38, fluid lactate dehydrogenase 72 (below 148): a transudate. Gram stain, culture and cytology negative.

studies.why: Below 100 rules out acute heart failure; above 400 makes heart failure likely, and above 900 acute heart failure.
studies.expect: About 1,100: acute heart failure likely.

studies.why: Sets the ejection fraction (below 40% is systolic, reduced-ejection-fraction failure) and the cause.
studies.expect: Dilated left ventricle with an akinetic anterior wall; ejection fraction about 30%; normal right ventricle and valves.

plan: Ultrasound-guided right thoracentesis, diagnostic and therapeutic: drain enough to ease his breathing, send the fluid tests with serum protein and lactate dehydrogenase the same day, and take a chest X-ray afterward for a pneumothorax.

A transudate is managed by treating the underlying disorder. Admit him: new reduced-ejection-fraction failure, decompensated (natriuretic peptide above 900, saturation 93%, waking up gasping). Give a loop diuretic (furosemide or bumetanide) through a vein, and oxygen for his hypoxemia.

Optimize his reduced-ejection-fraction medicines as he is hemodynamically stable: keep the beta blocker (metoprolol succinate); replace lisinopril with an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (sacubitril-valsartan), which is prioritized; add a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone) and a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin).
Follow potassium and kidney function daily on the diuretic and the new medicines.
Cardiology: cardiac rehabilitation, and a repeat echocardiogram once his medicines are optimized; an implantable defibrillator if the ejection fraction stays at 35% or less.
Repeat chest X-ray once he is diuresed: an effusion that stays or grows despite treatment of the heart failure needs another look for another cause.
education: Your heart muscle is pumping weakly, most likely from the damage your heart attack left, so fluid backs up into your lungs, your legs and the space around your right lung. That fluid presses on the lung, which is why you get winded and cannot lie flat.
The fluid we drained was the thin, watery kind that comes from pressure. The tests on it found no infection and no cancer cells.
You will stay in the hospital for a few days while medicine through a vein pulls the extra fluid off, and we start the heart medicines that help a weak heart work better and help you live longer.
Once you are home, take every heart medicine every day, weigh yourself every morning, go easy on salt, and call us if your weight climbs or your ankles swell again.
Come back at once for breathlessness at rest, waking up gasping again, chest pain like your heart attack, fainting, or a fever with sharp chest pain.
red_flags: Breathlessness at rest, or at night that does not settle on sitting up
Fever, chills or sharp chest pain with breathing (possible infected fluid)
Chest pain like his heart attack, or fainting
key.follow_up: Admission now for diuresis through a vein and medicine optimization; after discharge, cardiology follow-up with cardiac rehabilitation, a repeat echocardiogram once his medicines are optimized (a defibrillator if the ejection fraction stays at 35% or less), and a repeat chest X-ray to confirm the effusions have cleared.
key.presentation: Mr. Lindqvist is a 67-year-old man with hypertension, a heart attack with a stent eight years ago and a 41 pack-year former smoking history, presenting with three weeks of worsening exertional breathlessness, now after half a block. He sleeps on three pillows, woke up gasping last night, and has a dry night cough, ankle swelling and a nine-pound weight gain. He denies fever, sputum, coughing up blood, night sweats, liver disease and cancer. Saturation is 93%, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 132/80. The right base lags, with absent fremitus, dullness, a high, barely moving diaphragm, absent breath sounds and egophony above the fluid; the trachea is midline. He has a third heart sound and 2+ ankle edema. My differential is a heart failure effusion, malignant and parapneumonic effusions, and a low-albumin transudate. X-ray, ultrasound, thoracentesis, natriuretic peptide and echocardiogram show a transudate and an ejection fraction of 30%. Diagnosis: transudative effusion from heart failure. Plan: admit, loop diuretic, optimize heart failure medicines.

high_yield.item: Ask about orthopnea, waking up short of breath, leg swelling and weight gain
high_yield.why: Leg swelling, orthopnea and waking up short of breath point to heart failure as the cause of an effusion.

high_yield.item: Ask the effusion history: heart disease, liver disease, cancer, trauma and asbestos
high_yield.why: Each points to a cause; malignant effusions can appear years after a cancer diagnosis.

high_yield.item: Ask about fever, purulent sputum, coughing up blood, night sweats and weight loss
high_yield.why: Fever, purulent sputum and pleuritic pain suggest pneumonia; coughing up blood suggests malignancy; night sweats, coughing up blood and weight loss suggest tuberculosis.

high_yield.item: Percuss the back side to side, then measure diaphragmatic excursion
high_yield.why: Dullness over the fluid and a high level that barely moves (normal excursion is about 3 to 5.5 centimeters) mark the effusion and its top.

high_yield.item: Palpate fremitus and listen over and just above the fluid, with the voice sounds
high_yield.why: Over fluid, fremitus, breath sounds and voice sounds are decreased or absent; at the top, bronchial breath sounds and louder voice sounds may appear. Effusions under 300 milliliters give no findings, which is why the small left one is silent.

high_yield.item: Check the trachea
high_yield.why: A shift away from the effusion means a large one, over 1,000 milliliters; his is midline.

high_yield.item: Apply Light's criteria out loud
high_yield.why: Exudate if any one is met: fluid-to-serum protein above 0.5, fluid-to-serum lactate dehydrogenase above 0.6, or fluid lactate dehydrogenase above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum; transudate if none. Heart failure causes more than 90% of transudates.

exam.position: He sits on the edge of the exam table with the gown open at the back, leaning a little to the right and pressing a hand to his right upper chest when he coughs.

exam.thorax-inspect: The chest is symmetric, with no deformities, lesions or bruising, but the right upper chest moves less than the left with each breath. No retractions.
exam.breathing-pattern: Fast and shallow at about 24 breaths a minute, regular, cutting each deep breath short because of right-sided pain. Normal expiratory phase.
exam.expansion: Asymmetric: the right thumb moves less and lags behind the left when he takes a deep breath, and the breath catches with pain on the right.
exam.fremitus: Increased tactile fremitus over the right upper chest, below the clavicle in front and over the upper right back. Normal and symmetric over the rest of the chest, including both bases.
exam.percuss-anterior: Dull over the right upper anterior chest, from the clavicle down to about the 4th rib. Resonant below that and over the whole left side.
exam.percuss-posterior: Dull over the upper right back, above the level of the spine of the scapula. Resonant below that, at both bases and over the whole left side.

exam.ausc-posterior: Upper right back: bronchial breath sounds with late inspiratory crackles. Vesicular and clear at both bases and over the whole left side. No wheeze, no pleural rub.
exam.egophony: Present over the right upper lobe, front and back: "ee" is heard as "ay". Absent elsewhere.
exam.bronchophony: Present over the right upper lobe, front and back: "ninety-nine" is louder and clearer. Muffled and indistinct elsewhere.

plan: Severity: no major criterion for severe pneumonia (no shock needing vasopressors, no need for ventilation). Pneumonia Severity Index 58 points (male, age 58, nothing else), class II with 0.6% mortality; CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) 0, low severity. With clinical judgment (saturation 95%, alert, drinking, his wife at home), treat as an outpatient.

Outpatient regimen for a patient with a comorbidity (diabetes): amoxicillin/clavulanate, cefpodoxime or cefuroxime plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin) alone; review allergies, the QT interval, interactions and fluoroquinolone risks.
At least 3 days and until clinically stable; a course shorter than 5 days may be enough in nonsevere pneumonia. No routine corticosteroids and no routine cultures.
Supportive care: fluids, acetaminophen for fever and pain, rest, and closer blood sugar checks while he is sick.

Vaccines once he has recovered from this illness: one dose of 20- or 21-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (all adults 50 or older who never had one), the annual influenza vaccine and the updated COVID-19 vaccine.
Close follow-up (for example a recheck in 2 to 3 days) with return precautions: emergency department for breathlessness at rest, confusion, fainting, less urine or not keeping fluids or pills down.
education: You have pneumonia, an infection in the upper part of your right lung. The X-ray shows it, and it matches what I hear with the stethoscope.
Your severity scores are low, so you can be treated at home with antibiotic pills. Take every dose, even once you feel better.
Drink plenty, rest, use acetaminophen for the fever and the side pain, and check your sugar more often while you're sick, because infection pushes it up.
Once you're over this, get the pneumonia shot and this year's flu and COVID shots: they protect against severe illness.

We'll check on you closely, for example in 2 to 3 days. Come back sooner or go to the emergency department if your breathing gets harder, you get confused, you can't keep fluids or pills down, or you are not improving or get better and then worse.
red_flags: Breathlessness at rest or a falling oxygen level
Confusion, fainting or less urine
Unable to keep fluids or the antibiotic down
Not improving, or better and then worse
key.follow_up: Close follow-up with return precautions, for example a recheck in 2 to 3 days by phone or in clinic, to confirm he is improving and taking the antibiotics; if he worsens, reassess the diagnosis, adherence and resistance and look for an effusion, empyema or abscess.
key.presentation: Mr. Mensah is a 58-year-old letter carrier with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and a 20 pack-year former smoking history, presenting with three days of fever to 102.6, shaking chills, a cough with yellow-green sputum and sharp right-sided pain on deep breaths, after a cold from his grandson. He is winded on stairs. He denies coughing up blood, leg swelling, travel, orthopnea and confusion. Temperature 102.2, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 24, blood pressure 134/82, saturation 95% on room air. He looks ill and splints his right side. Over the right upper lobe, front and back, fremitus is increased and percussion is dull, with bronchial breath sounds, late inspiratory crackles and egophony. My differential is community-acquired pneumonia, bronchitis, influenza and pulmonary embolism. I would order a chest X-ray, metabolic panel and influenza and COVID-19 test. Pneumonia Severity Index 58, class II; CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) zero. Working diagnosis: nonsevere right upper lobe pneumonia, treated at home with amoxicillin/clavulanate plus azithromycin.

high_yield.item: Ask the color of the sputum and whether there is blood

high_yield.item: Ask about leg swelling, calf pain, travel, immobility, surgery and orthopnea
high_yield.why: Keeps pulmonary embolism and heart failure on the differential of breathlessness with chest pain.

high_yield.item: Ask the chronic conditions and check his mental status

high_yield.item: Palpate expansion and tactile fremitus, side to side
high_yield.why: A lagging right side with increased fremitus over the right upper lobe means consolidation.

high_yield.item: Percuss and listen over the upper lobes front and back, then test egophony, bronchophony and whispered pectoriloquy
high_yield.why: Dullness, bronchial breath sounds, late inspiratory crackles and positive voice sounds over one lobe; with fever and cough, bronchial breath sounds and egophony more than triple the likelihood of pneumonia.

high_yield.item: Interpret the vital signs and score the severity out loud
high_yield.why: Pneumonia Severity Index 58 (class II, 0.6% mortality), CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) 0, saturation 95%: nonsevere, suitable for treatment at home with clinical judgment.

Notify the local or state tuberculosis program of presumed tuberculosis today; her grandchildren and other close contacts need prompt public-health assessment.

Microbiology: three sputum specimens 8 to 24 hours apart (one early-morning) for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, a rapid molecular test on at least one, molecular and culture-based drug-susceptibility testing, and a human immunodeficiency virus test; the persistent, painless cervical node can be extrapulmonary tuberculosis and may need its own specimen.

Treatment with the program: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin; ethambutol stops once susceptibility to isoniazid and rifampin is established; daily directly observed therapy, in person or by video.

Monitoring: at least monthly review of adherence, symptoms and side effects; sputum cultures until they convert, with the response documented at 2 months; watch for liver injury and drug interactions.
Address her risks for progression: smoking cessation and better control of her diabetes.
education: This looks like tuberculosis, a lung infection that spreads through the air when you cough, talk or sing. It is curable.
Until the health department says you can't spread it, stay home from work, keep visitors away, especially your grandkids, and wear a mask around anyone else.
Treatment is several pills every day for about six months, and a nurse watches you take them, in person or by video. Taking every dose is what cures it.
The health department will check your family and other close contacts, and the little ones will be seen quickly.
Tell us right away if you cough up more than streaks of blood, get short of breath, get a bad headache or stiff neck, or your skin or eyes turn yellow on the medicines.
red_flags: Coughing up more than streaks of blood
Breathlessness at rest
Headache, stiff neck or confusion
Signs of liver injury on treatment
key.follow_up: Close and long: the tuberculosis program and the clinic see her at least monthly through six months of directly observed therapy, with sputum cultures until they convert and the response documented at 2 months; isolation ends only when the program clears her.
key.presentation: Ms. Novak is a 52-year-old corrections officer with type 2 diabetes and a 30 pack-year current smoking history, presenting with two months of daily cough, blood-streaked twice this week, evening fevers, drenching night sweats and a 14-pound weight loss. About 15 months ago an inmate on her unit had tuberculosis; her skin test then was negative and she missed the repeat. She denies travel and immunosuppressing medicines. Temperature 100.4, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 18, saturation 96% on room air; she looks thin. Over the right upper lobe, front and back, percussion is dull and fremitus increased, with bronchial breath sounds and crackles; there are crackles at the left apex and a right cervical node. My differential is pulmonary tuberculosis, lung cancer, nontuberculous mycobacterial disease and lung abscess. I would mask her and order a chest X-ray, three sputum specimens for smear, culture and rapid molecular testing, an interferon-gamma release assay and a human immunodeficiency virus test. Working diagnosis: active pulmonary tuberculosis; notify the tuberculosis program.

high_yield.item: Ask how long the cough has lasted and whether there is blood
high_yield.why: Two months of daily cough is chronic; blood streaks are enough, since dramatic hemoptysis is not required for tuberculosis.

high_yield.item: Ask about fevers, night sweats, weight loss and appetite
high_yield.why: Fever, night sweats and weight loss with fatigue are the systemic picture of pulmonary tuberculosis.

high_yield.item: Take the exposure history: the jail, the inmate with tuberculosis and the repeat test she missed
high_yield.why: Close contact and enclosed, poorly ventilated workplaces are exposure risks; early infection can give a negative test, so it is repeated 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure.

high_yield.item: Ask the risks for progression: human immunodeficiency virus, immunosuppressing drugs, diabetes, smoking, alcohol
high_yield.why: Recent infection within 2 years, diabetes and tobacco use all raise her risk of progressing to disease.

high_yield.item: Mask her and wear an N95 as soon as tuberculosis is suspected
high_yield.why: Infectious pulmonary tuberculosis needs immediate airborne precautions.

high_yield.item: Percuss and listen over the upper lobes front and back, and feel for lymph nodes
high_yield.why: Post-primary disease favors the upper lobes; crackles, bronchial breath sounds and lymphadenopathy are clues, though a normal examination does not exclude tuberculosis. A persistent, painless node can be extrapulmonary tuberculosis and may need its own specimen.

high_yield.item: Order three sputum specimens, not only a skin or blood test
high_yield.why: The skin and blood tests show infection, not disease; the sputum smears, culture and rapid molecular test make the diagnosis.

high_yield.item: Report to the tuberculosis program and ask who lives with or visits her
high_yield.why: Presumed tuberculosis is reported; young children who are contacts need prompt assessment.

door.name: Tyler Whitfield
door.cc: My chest hurts and I can't catch my breath.

cases.persona: A 27-year-old computer support worker, tall and lanky, polite and a little embarrassed to be here, who keeps saying he 'probably just pulled something'. He sits very still, takes small breaths, keeps his left arm close to his side, and pauses briefly between sentences when a breath catches. His father's old story has him quietly worried, and he keeps coming back to a wedding trip he has planned.
cases.opening: I got this sharp pain in the left side of my chest last night, and I still can't take a full breath.

I had to stop halfway up the one flight of stairs to my apartment this morning. Normally I take them two at a time.
Yes, that's the main thing. Every deep breath stabs.
No. I've always been skinny, and my weight hasn't changed.
Orthopnea and waking up short of breath
Lying flat hurt, so I propped myself up, but it wasn't my breathing. I never woke up gasping.
No flights or long drives lately, and no surgery.
Nobody around me has been sick.

My heart's been beating a little fast since this started, but it's steady. No pressure in my chest, no fainting, no swelling.
No sore throat, no stuffy nose.
No asthma or anything like that. Nobody's ever told me something was wrong with my lungs.
None. My wrist was just a cast.
I don't take any regular medicines.
Two ibuprofen last night, around ten. Nothing else, no supplements.
About half a pack a day since I was eighteen, so nine years. I keep meaning to quit.
I vaped for a while in college but stopped. No weed.
A few beers on the weekend.
I do computer support for an insurance company, at a desk. No dust or chemicals.
A second-floor apartment. No mold, no pets.
I live with my girlfriend, Maya. She's at work; she's the one who told me to come in.
I think I'm up to date. I got a flu shot at work last month.
Never been around it that I know of, and I've never been tested.
My mom's healthy. She takes a pill for her thyroid.

That something's really wrong with my lung. And I'm supposed to fly to a friend's wedding in three weeks.

Pickup basketball on Sundays. I haven't played since this past Sunday, and I felt fine then.

questions: Is my lung going to be okay?
Do I really have to go to the hospital?
Can I still fly to my friend's wedding in three weeks?

exam.position: He sits up on the edge of the exam table with the gown open at the back, holding his left arm close to his side.
exam.general-survey: Alert, tall and thin, in mild distress from pain, breathing a little fast but speaking in full sentences. No audible wheeze or stridor. Normal color, no sweating.
exam.thorax-inspect: The chest has no deformity, wound or bruising. The left side moves less than the right with each breath (a left-sided lag). No retractions.
exam.breathing-pattern: Slightly fast at 22 breaths per minute, regular and shallow; he takes small breaths because a deep one hurts. Normal expiratory phase.
exam.chest-wall-palp: No tenderness, deformity, masses or crepitus over the posterior, lateral or anterior chest wall, and no crackling under the skin of the chest or neck. Pressing on the left chest wall does not reproduce his pain.
exam.expansion: Asymmetric: the left thumb moves less than the right with a deep breath.
exam.fremitus: Decreased to absent over the left chest posteriorly, laterally and anteriorly, most of all over the upper left chest. Normal on the right.
exam.percuss-posterior: Posterior chest: hyperresonant over the whole left back, most over the upper and middle part; resonant over the right back.
exam.percuss-lateral: Lateral chest: hyperresonant on the left; resonant on the right.
exam.percuss-anterior: Anterior chest: hyperresonant, almost drum-like (tympanic), over the left upper chest; resonant over the right upper lobe.
exam.ausc-posterior: Posterior chest: breath sounds markedly diminished over the upper and middle left back and distant at the left base; vesicular over the right back. No crackles, wheezes or rub.
exam.ausc-lateral: Lateral chest: breath sounds markedly diminished on the left; vesicular on the right. No crackles, wheezes or rub.
exam.ausc-anterior: Anterior chest: breath sounds nearly absent over the left upper chest; vesicular over the right upper lobe. No crackles, wheezes or rub.
exam.bronchophony: Voice sounds are decreased over the left chest: "ninety-nine" is fainter on the left than the right. No bronchophony.
exam.trachea: The trachea is midline, with no shift to the right. The neck veins are not distended.
exam.heart-ausc: Regular rhythm, fast at about 104. Normal first and second heart sounds, with no murmur, rub, extra heart sound or crunching sound in time with the heartbeat.

tests.name: Chest X-ray (upright)
tests.result: A thin, sharp visceral pleural line at the left apex, convex toward the chest wall and running down the left lateral chest, with no lung markings beyond it. Apex-to-cupola distance 4 centimeters: a large pneumothorax. Trachea and mediastinum midline; right lung clear; no effusion or rib fracture.
tests.cap: An example, not his own film. The yellow box holds three small arrows at the left apex, which its source labels apical subpleural blebs. A pneumothorax shows as a thin visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it; his left one is 4 centimeters from the apex to the top of the chest cavity.

tests.name: Electrocardiogram (12-lead)
tests.result: Sinus tachycardia at 104. Normal axis and intervals; no ST elevation or depression.

tests.name: Complete blood count (CBC)
tests.result: Normal: white blood cell count 7,900, hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, platelets normal.

tests.name: Computed tomography (CT) of the chest
tests.result: Not available in this urgent care: it is done in a hospital imaging department.

tests.name: Point-of-care chest ultrasound
tests.result: Not available in this urgent care: there is no bedside ultrasound machine here.

tests.name: Arterial blood gas
tests.result: Not available in this urgent care: arterial blood gases are run in a hospital laboratory.

tests.name: Troponin
tests.result: Not available in this urgent care: it is sent to a hospital laboratory.

tests.name: D-dimer
tests.result: Normal: below 500 nanograms per milliliter.

key.diagnosis: Large left primary spontaneous pneumothorax (apex-to-cupola distance 4 centimeters), clinically stable: it needs a chest tube, which this urgent care cannot place, so he goes to the emergency department now
must_not_miss: Tension pneumothorax: a trachea shifting to the right, a falling blood pressure or distended neck veins means needle decompression at once, without waiting for an X-ray
Pulmonary embolism, the other cause of sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness: it is set aside only because the X-ray shows the pleural line that explains everything

ddx.name: Pneumothorax (primary spontaneous, large, left-sided, clinically stable)
ddx.support: Sudden sharp left pleuritic pain and breathlessness that began at rest, in a tall, thin 27-year-old man who smokes and whose father had a collapsed lung. Heart rate 104 and saturation 94%. The left side lags, with decreased fremitus, hyperresonance and diminished breath and voice sounds, and the upright X-ray shows a visceral pleural line 4 centimeters from the apex.
ddx.against: Nothing against it. No lung disease, so it is primary; no trauma or procedure; the trachea is midline and the blood pressure normal, so it is not under tension.

ddx.name: Pulmonary embolism
ddx.support: Sudden breathlessness with pleuritic chest pain, a heart rate of 104 and a saturation of 94%.
ddx.against: No leg swelling, travel, surgery or coughing up blood; hyperresonance with absent fremitus is air in the pleural space, and the X-ray shows the pneumothorax.

ddx.name: Myocardial infarction
ddx.support: Sudden chest pain with breathlessness and a fast heart rate in a smoker.
ddx.against: He is 27; the pain is sharp, one-sided and worse with each breath rather than pressure with exertion, and the electrocardiogram has no ST changes.

ddx.name: Costochondritis or chest wall strain
ddx.support: Sharp, localized chest pain that is worse with movement.
ddx.against: Pressing on the chest wall does not reproduce the pain, and the lag, hyperresonance and absent breath sounds point inside the chest.

studies.why: The initial test: it shows the visceral pleural line (thin, sharp, convex toward the chest wall, no lung markings beyond it) and sizes the pneumothorax by the apex-to-cupola distance, under 3 centimeters small and 3 or more large, which sets the treatment.
studies.expect: A left visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it; apex-to-cupola distance 4 centimeters (large); trachea and mediastinum midline.

studies.why: Myocardial infarction and pericarditis are on every sudden chest pain differential.
studies.expect: Sinus tachycardia at 104; no ST elevation or depression.

studies.test: Computed tomography of the chest, later in the hospital
studies.why: The best test for the presence, size and location of the air, and it finds apical blebs or bullae and any underlying lung disease; impractical when time is critical, so not first.
studies.expect: Large left pneumothorax with small blebs at the left apex; no underlying lung disease.

plan: Stable by the stability definition (respiratory rate under 24, heart rate between 60 and 120, normal blood pressure, room-air saturation above 90%, whole sentences), but large (4 centimeters at the apex) with significant pain and breathlessness: it needs chest tube insertion. Catheter aspiration or a small-bore catheter is also accepted for a symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax with no contraindication. This urgent care can do none of them.

Transfer to the emergency department now by ambulance; until it arrives, oxygen at 100% by non-rebreather mask (it speeds resorption of the air), pain control, and repeated checks of his vital signs and trachea.

In the emergency department: a chest tube at the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line, a chest X-ray afterward to confirm the lung has re-expanded, chest computed tomography for apical blebs, and video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery if the air leak persists or the lung will not expand.

If he turns unstable (falling blood pressure, trachea shifting to the right, distended neck veins), it is a tension pneumothorax: needle decompression in the left second intercostal space, midclavicular line, over the third rib, then a chest tube.
Smoking cessation, with help if he is willing to quit; video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis if it ever comes back.
education: A small blister on the top of your left lung popped and let air leak into the space around the lung, so part of the lung has collapsed. You did not cause it; it happens most in tall, thin young men, and smoking makes it more likely.
It is too big to wait out. The emergency department will put a small tube between your ribs to let the air out so the lung can open back up. We cannot do that here, so an ambulance will take you now.

It comes back in close to half of people within three years, usually on the same side. Quitting smoking is the biggest thing you can do to lower that risk, and if it does come back, a keyhole operation can seal the lung so it stops happening.
No flying until a chest X-ray shows your lung is fully back up, and then wait another 1 to 2 weeks; ask before you book the wedding flight. Do not scuba dive.
Call 911 or come straight back if your breathing suddenly gets worse, you feel faint, or the pain gets much worse.
red_flags: Breathing that suddenly gets worse
Feeling faint or a falling blood pressure
The trachea shifting to the right or the neck veins swelling (tension pneumothorax)
key.follow_up: Emergency: ambulance to the emergency department now for a chest tube; then follow-up chest X-rays to confirm the lung has fully re-expanded, a surgical evaluation if the air leak lasts more than 4 days, and surgery to prevent recurrence if it ever comes back.
key.presentation: Mr. Whitfield is a 27-year-old man who smokes half a pack a day, whose father had a collapsed lung, presenting with sudden sharp left-sided chest pain and breathlessness that began at rest last night. The pain stabs with every deep breath and cough, and one flight of stairs now winds him. He denies trauma, fever, sputum, coughing up blood, leg swelling, travel, prior episodes and fainting. Heart rate is 104, respiratory rate 22, saturation 94% on room air, blood pressure 124/76: stable. He is tall and thin and speaks in full sentences. The left chest lags, with decreased fremitus, hyperresonance and diminished breath and voice sounds; the trachea is midline. My differential is pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction and chest wall pain. The upright chest X-ray shows a large left pneumothorax, 4 centimeters apex to cupola, and the electrocardiogram sinus tachycardia only. Diagnosis: large left primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Plan: oxygen, pain control, ambulance to the emergency department for a chest tube, and smoking cessation.

high_yield.item: Ask what he was doing when it started, and about any trauma or chest procedure
high_yield.why: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax often starts at rest; trauma or a procedure makes it traumatic or iatrogenic, which changes the treatment.

high_yield.item: Ask about smoking, body build, family history and prior episodes
high_yield.why: Tall, thin men aged 20 to 40, smoking (a significant risk factor) and family history; recurrence is common, and a recurrence goes to surgery.

high_yield.item: Ask about underlying lung disease
high_yield.why: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or another lung disease makes it secondary: less reserve, more dangerous, a chest tube and hospital admission.

high_yield.item: Compare the two sides: expansion, fremitus, percussion and breath and voice sounds
high_yield.why: Decreased expansion, decreased or absent fremitus, hyperresonance and diminished breath and voice sounds on one side are the pneumothorax pattern; dullness would mean fluid instead.

high_yield.item: Check the trachea and neck veins and recheck the blood pressure
high_yield.why: Tension pneumothorax shifts the trachea away from the collapsed lung, distends the neck veins and drops the blood pressure: a clinical diagnosis treated by needle decompression at the second intercostal space, midclavicular line.

high_yield.item: Apply the stability definition out loud
high_yield.why: Respiratory rate under 24, heart rate 60 to 120, normal blood pressure, room-air saturation above 90% and whole sentences: he meets all five, so he is stable for transfer.

high_yield.item: Size it on the upright X-ray and match the treatment to the size and symptoms
high_yield.why: Small (under 3 centimeters) with few symptoms is observed with oxygen and a repeat film; large with significant symptoms needs a chest tube, which means the emergency department.

high_yield.item: Counsel on recurrence, smoking and flying
high_yield.why: Recurrence approaches 50% within three years; quitting smoking lowers the risk; air travel waits until an X-ray confirms full re-expansion, then 1 to 2 weeks; no scuba diving.
